opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think we're closer than most people assume, but further than the hype videos suggest. Those two things are both true at the same time.

Hardware has come a long way. Actuators are cheaper, batteries are better, and you can now build a bipedal platform that walks reliably and doesn't fall over every time someone bumps it. Ten years ago that alone was a research milestone. Today it's close to table stakes.

The real gap is in the intelligence layer, specifically dexterous manipulation and generalization. Getting a robot to pick up one specific part on one specific line is a solved problem; industrial arms have done that for decades. Getting a humanoid to walk into a warehouse it's never seen, figure out which tote matters, handle a slightly crushed box, and recover when something goes wrong, without an engineer babysitting it, is the hard part. That's where the large foundation models and learning from demonstration are starting to make a real difference, but reliability matters. A demo that works 90% of the time is impressive on YouTube. In a factory, 90% means it fails constantly.

So my view is that over the next couple of years you'll see humanoids doing real, paid work in fairly structured settings: logistics, manufacturing, moving materials, machine tending. These are places where the environment is built for humans, so the humanoid form factor actually earns its keep, but the variability is bounded. The home, elder care, truly unstructured environments are a longer road. Those demand a level of safety, robustness, and common sense we're not at yet.

The thing I'd tell people to watch isn't the flashiest demo. It's uptime, interventions per hour, and cost per task. When those numbers start to look like a human worker's, adoption happens fast. We're not there broadly yet, but for certain narrow jobs we're getting very close.

r001.rationale: The candidate says paid humanoid work in structured settings may appear over the next couple of years and that broad adoption is not here yet; it does not state they are already working full shifts in real-world deployments.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say closer than most people think in some ways, and further than the demos suggest in others.

If you watch the videos coming out of the big humanoid companies, it looks like we're a year or two away from robots doing laundry and stocking shelves. And the hardware really has gotten remarkable. The actuators, the batteries, the balance controllers, all of that has improved enormously in the last five years. Walking is close to solved. Getting up off the floor, going up stairs, even some running, that's largely there.

The hard part is still manipulation and reliability. Walking is a problem you can mostly solve in simulation because physics is physics. Picking up a crumpled bag, or a wet plate, or a box that's heavier on one side than you expected, that's a problem where the real world keeps surprising you. And in a factory or a warehouse, the bar isn't "it worked in the demo." The bar is that it works ten thousand times in a row, overnight, without a person standing behind it ready to catch it. We're not at that bar yet for general tasks.

So my honest answer is that you'll see humanoids doing narrow, structured work in real facilities over the next couple of years. Moving totes, tending a machine, repetitive handling in a controlled space, often with a human in the loop or teleoperation behind the scenes. That's real, and it's happening now in pilots. The general-purpose robot that walks into an arbitrary home and is useful, that's further out. I'd guess the better part of a decade before that's something ordinary people are buying.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that it's all about the robot. A lot of what makes a deployment succeed is the boring stuff: the environment, the safety case, the data pipeline, the cost per hour compared to a person. The companies that figure out those pieces will get there first, even if their robot isn't the flashiest one on YouTube.

r001.rationale: The response says narrow, structured work is happening now in pilots, often with human help, and says robots are not yet reliable enough for general tasks. It does not state that they are working full shifts in real-world deployments.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by working in the real world. If you mean doing a specific task in a controlled environment, we’re close. If you mean walking into an unfamiliar building and doing all the things a person can do, that’s a much harder problem.

The gap is between a demonstration and something a customer can rely on every day. Can it work for an entire shift? Can it handle something being in the wrong place? And when it gets confused, can it fail safely? Those are the questions that determine whether you have a useful product.

So I expect adoption to start with narrow jobs in predictable environments. You don’t need a robot that can do everything. You need one that can do a valuable task consistently, at a cost that makes sense.

r001.rationale: The candidate poses working an entire shift as an open question and does not say humanoid robots are already doing so in real-world deployments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by working in the real world. If we mean doing a specific task in a controlled environment, we’re pretty close. If we mean walking into an unfamiliar workplace and doing whatever a person needs done, that’s a much harder problem.

The challenge is reliability. A robot can do something impressive once, but can it do it all day, safely, around people, at a cost that makes sense? That’s the threshold that matters. I think we’ll see humanoids take on narrow jobs first, with broader capabilities coming as they prove themselves.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliability as a threshold and says humanoids will take on narrow jobs first; it does not say they are already working full shifts in real-world deployments.
